summaries.summary: Writing errors take many forms, automatic identification is challenging with limited annotated data, and Rei2016 found additional training data most improves performance.
Realistic artificial data could create annotated error examples and anonymise source corpora, but naive error generation may produce unnatural errors and misleading patterns.
Previous AEG work targeted specific error types, with Felice2014a covering only five types and 35.74% of errors in the CoNLL 2014 training dataset.
The paper investigates SMT-based and pattern-based supervised AEG for all error types, improving two benchmarks and yielding 4.3% absolute improvement in INLINEFORM0 when combined.
Two AEG methods modify correct text, align alternative sentences using Levenshtein distance to mark errors, and may use more advanced alignment methods in future work.
In Section SECREF4, the automatically labeled data is used for training error detection models.
AEG is treated as translation from correct sentences to likely errors, motivated by SMT context patterns and prior reverse and round-trip translation work.
A phrase-based SMT error generation system uses Pialign, character-level Levenshtein distance, Moses, IRSTLM Toolkit, and a 5-gram language model with modified Kneser-Ney smoothing.
A pattern-based AEG method extracts word and POS-tag patterns from annotated corrections, extending Felice2014a beyond 5 error types to all types.
Aligned original and corrected sentences yield short (incorrect phrase, correct phrase) patterns with up to one context token and word forms or POS tags.
An example uses `We went shop on Saturday' and `We went shopping on Saturday' to produce a pattern.
The example pattern is (VVD shop_VV0 II, VVD shopping_VVG II).
Reversed patterns with frequency INLINEFORM0 yield 35,625 patterns, generate sampled errors while balancing error types and sentence proportions, and use RASP with the CLAWS2 tagset.
A neural sequence labeling model uses word embeddings, a bidirectional LSTM, feedforward layer, softmax, categorical cross-entropy, and AdaDelta for token-level error detection.
Error generation models trained on the public FCE training set used corrected FCE text (450K tokens) and English Vocabulary Profile sentences (270K tokens).
Detection models were evaluated on FCE test data (41K tokens) and two CoNLL 2014 Shared Task annotations (30K tokens), with 3 artificial data versions per system.
Table TABREF4 reports results using INLINEFORM0, while INLINEFORM1 weights precision twice as much as recall, with comparison to Rei2016 on the same FCE dataset.
Artificial data substantially improved error detection, all-error-type PAT and MT methods outperformed FY14, and Ann+PAT+MT gave the best overall performance on all datasets.
Approximate Randomisation Test BIBREF17, BIBREF18 showed artificial-data improvements were significant, and the final combination significantly outperformed Felice2014a on all three datasets.
Figure FIGREF6 shows INLINEFORM0 improves on the development set when multiple SMT n-best translations provide alternative versions of the same input text.
Prior AEG research addressed specific error types or limited edit operations, while this work explored two holistic AEG approaches that significantly improved error detection performance.
The paper investigated pattern-based AEG from annotated corpora and an MT framework translating grammatically correct sentences into incorrect sentences.
Artificial data improved all generation methods on three annotations using FCE and CoNLL 2014, with all-error-type patterns outperforming Felice2014a and combined PAT and MT best on all datasets.
